title: O5 – Incentives: Hawthorne, March & Simon, Hirschman, Etzioni

blocks.text: Incentives answer the question: why do people contribute to an organisation, and how can it steer their behaviour?
Hawthorne (Mayo): social factors – attention, group morale, informal norms – matter more than physical working conditions.

March & Simon: people stay as long as retributions ≥ contributions – as they perceive them (psychological contract). If the balance breaks, they reduce contributions or increase retributions themselves.
Hirschman: when an organisation no longer meets people's expectations they react by exit, voice, exit & voice or loyalty.
Etzioni: organisations combine three incentive and control mechanisms – coercion (stick), remuneration (carrot) and identification (heart).

Harvard team at Western Electric's Hawthorne plant (Chicago) tested the effect of lighting, breaks, working hours, heat or talking on productivity – expecting, as scientific management predicts, that better conditions raise output.
Surprise: productivity rose whatever was changed (more or less light, longer or shorter breaks).

Feeling observed changes behaviour · showing people you care raises performance · affective relations, group morale and informal leaders matter – the informal organisation counts more than the formal one · groups set strict informal rules (don't produce too much or too little, never tell the boss anything that harms a member, don't play the boss).
Comes from outside the individual: money, grades, rewards.
Comes from within: the reward is doing the task itself (accomplishment, pleasure, meaning).
When a daycare introduced a fine for parents who picked up their children late, lateness increased: a moral obligation turned into a price – extrinsic incentives can crowd out intrinsic motives.
People stay in an organisation as long as retributions ≥ contributions (psychological contract).
Salary, status, work satisfaction, personal development, social interactions, power, meaning …
Working time, effort, subordination, expertise, skills …

Both can be material or immaterial; what counts is the subjective, sometimes symbolic perception, not the objective value (weekend work feels very costly; using company property privately feels worth more than its price).
If the balance breaks, people restore it by reducing contributions (lateness, absenteeism) or increasing retributions (theft, fraudulent expenses).

Google exercise: high retributions (pay, prestige, perks, interesting problems) but also high contributions (workload, availability at night, pressure, conformism) and some missing retributions (recognition, promotion, meaning for non-stars).
Leave silently – possible when an external labour market exists.
Leave and voice concerns – can harm the firm's reputation.
Stay and protest, hoping management will change things.
Stay and accept – out of loyalty or out of resignation and lack of alternatives.
Two axes: stay vs leave × keep silent vs complain.

sections.heading: Etzioni (1961): three incentive and control mechanisms

blocks.text: Coercive power: control and sanctions – punishments (the stick).
Remunerative power: compensation and promises – rewards (the carrot).
Symbolic (normative) power: belonging, vision, values – the heart.
Organisations use all three in variable proportions; the mix must fit the kind of work and people.
